newsitem.title: COLOMBIA: Colombia says drug move is not anti-U.S. reprisal.
newsitem.headline: Colombia says drug move is not anti-U.S. reprisal.

text.p: Colombia quietly suspended aerial spraying of illicit drug crops on Wednesday, but top officials stressed the move was not a reprisal for the U.S. decision to leave the country on a drugs blacklist.
Washington called for eradication operations to be resumed as soon as possible, saying it hoped the suspension had been taken for strictly technical reasons.

The decision came at a time when the U.S. government estimates the cultivation of coca leaf -- the raw material for cocaine -- has risen 32 percent in Colombia, making it the second-largest grower in the world.

"Cropdusting is fundamental in the fight against narco- trafficking and Colombia's decision was never to end the programme or suspend it indefinitely," Justice Minister Carlos Medellin told Reuters. "The move may create the impression that it was politically motivated but it is nothing like that."

He said Colombia would take a few days to compare its data on the spread of illicit drug crops with that obtained from U.S. satellite images and to look for ways to boost the effectiveness of the eradication programme.

Gen. Rosso Jose Serrano, head of the National Police, reiterated the suspension was to review the effectiveness of the programme but said it would not be terminated, describing aerial fumigation as the programme that "hurts narco-traffickers the most".

There was no formal announcement of the suspension, which came just two days after Colombian Interior Minister Horacio Serpa denied that the government had any plans to retaliate against Washington's "decertification" of Colombia.
But U.S. officials were quick to react to low-key comments by Joaquin Polo, head of the National Drug Policy office, in a radio interview, that the programme had been halted.

"We've not received any explanation for this decision ... We hope it has been taken for technical reasons only and not policy reasons. And we certainly urge a resumption of eradication operations as soon as possible," State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns told reporters in Washington.
